ch5_ex8_q1a: N...E bearings are the easy case: the true bearing is just the angle, padded to three digits. The NE quadrant covers $000^\circ$T to $090^\circ$T.
ch5_ex8_q1b: Picture a clock hand that starts at north and turns clockwise. To end up $20^\circ$ west of north it must go almost all the way round: $360^\circ - 20^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q1c: Quadrant ranges to memorise: NE $0$-$90$, SE $90$-$180$, SW $180$-$270$, NW $270$-$360$. S$35^\circ$W is in SW, so the answer must lie between 180 and 270.
ch5_ex8_q2a: S$x^\circ$E means start at south ($180^\circ$) and turn back towards east, so you go back $x^\circ$: $180^\circ - 28^\circ = 152^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q2b: Three-digit habit: writing $034^\circ$T rather than $34^\circ$T prevents misreading, the same reason pilots and sailors use it.
ch5_ex8_q2c: Start at south ($180^\circ$) and keep turning clockwise towards west, so add: $180^\circ + 42^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q3a: Under $090^\circ$T, the compass bearing is simply N$\theta$E with the same number.
ch5_ex8_q3b: Ask how far the bearing is from the nearer of N ($0^\circ$/$360^\circ$) or S ($180^\circ$). $132^\circ$ is $48^\circ$ short of south, on the east side.
ch5_ex8_q3c: Check by converting back: S$87^\circ$W gives $180^\circ + 87^\circ = 267^\circ$T. Reversing the conversion is a quick self-test.
ch5_ex8_q4a: $330^\circ$ is $30^\circ$ short of a full turn back to north, so it is $30^\circ$ west of north: N$30^\circ$W.
ch5_ex8_q4b: $086^\circ$T is just $4^\circ$ north of due east. Compass bearings still measure from N, so it is N$86^\circ$E, not E$4^\circ$N.
ch5_ex8_q4c: $234^\circ$ is between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$, so it is in the SW quadrant. Subtract $180^\circ$ to get the angle from south.
ch5_ex8_q5a: West of north is the anticlockwise side, so true bearing $= 360^\circ - 35^\circ$. Any path drawn up and to the left has a bearing between $270^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q5b: Below east means turning further clockwise past $090^\circ$, so add: $90^\circ + 22^\circ = 112^\circ$T.
ch5_ex8_q5c: Below west means short of west going clockwise, so subtract: $270^\circ - 35^\circ = 235^\circ$T. Check: it is in the SW range, 180 to 270.
ch5_ex8_q6a: Due east, south, west and north are always $090^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $270^\circ$ and $000^\circ$T. No calculation is needed.
ch5_ex8_q6b: An angle marked from south means the leg is S$65^\circ$E, so true bearing $= 180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ$T.
ch5_ex8_q6c: The first leg is N$50^\circ$W and the second is S$40^\circ$W. Converting each to a compass bearing first makes the true bearing easy: $360^\circ - 50^\circ$ and $180^\circ + 40^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q7a: A bearing just over $090^\circ$ (like $100^\circ$) points slightly below east on the page. Use the compass points as landmarks before measuring the exact angle.
ch5_ex8_q7b: $135^\circ$T is exactly south-east (halfway between E and S), and $240^\circ$T is $60^\circ$ past south, nearer to west than to south.
ch5_ex8_q8a: Landmark check: $260^\circ$ is $10^\circ$ short of west, $120^\circ$ is $30^\circ$ past east, and $032^\circ$ is about a third of the way from N to E.
ch5_ex8_q8b: Turn each compass bearing into a true bearing to check your sketch: N$40^\circ$W $= 320^\circ$, S$30^\circ$W $= 210^\circ$, S$50^\circ$E $= 130^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q8c: In true bearings these are $020^\circ$, $070^\circ$ and $150^\circ$. Each leg turns further clockwise, so the path curves round to the right.
ch5_ex8_q9a: Universal shortcut: for any true bearing $\theta$, east displacement $= d\sin\theta$ and north displacement $= d\cos\theta$. Negative results mean west or south, so this works in every quadrant.
ch5_ex8_q9b: Check: $13.38^2 + 14.86^2 \approx 400 = 20^2$. Also $42^\circ < 45^\circ$, so north should be bigger than east, and it is.
ch5_ex8_q9c: The return trip is the same line walked backwards, so it points exactly opposite: add or subtract $180^\circ$. The distance stays 20 km.
ch5_ex8_q9d: $130^\circ$T is $40^\circ$ past east, heading down-right. In the sketch, C ends up well to the east and south of A.
ch5_ex8_q9e: Using the shortcut: $80\cos 130^\circ \approx -51.42$. The negative sign tells you it is 51.42 km south.
ch5_ex8_q9g: $130^\circ + 180^\circ = 310^\circ$. Rule: if the original bearing is under 180, add 180; if it is over 180, subtract 180.
ch5_ex8_q10: For a compass bearing, just swap both letters: the reverse of N$35^\circ$E is S$35^\circ$W, which is $215^\circ$T.
ch5_ex8_q11: Both legs make $60^\circ$ with the north-south line ($240^\circ$ = S$60^\circ$W, $300^\circ$ = N$60^\circ$W), so west $= (0.7 + 1.3)\sin 60^\circ = 2 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}$.
That is why the answer is 1.732: it is $\sqrt{3}$ to 3 decimal places.
ch5_ex8_q12a: Shortcut: east $= 6\sin 120^\circ + 4\sin 80^\circ$. Type it straight into the calculator; no quadrant diagram is needed.
ch5_ex8_q12b: Shortcut: north $= 6\cos 120^\circ + 4\cos 80^\circ \approx -2.305$. The minus sign means south.
Exact value: $\cos 120^\circ = -\tfrac{1}{2}$, so the first leg goes exactly 3 km south.
ch5_ex8_q12c: The boat is far east and only a little south, so the bearing should be a bit more than $090^\circ$. $104^\circ 10'$ fits.
Bearing $= 90^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\text{south}}{\text{east}}\right)$ when the point is in the SE quadrant.
ch5_ex8_q13: Shortcut: north $= 450\cos 320^\circ + 130\cos 350^\circ + 330\cos 50^\circ$. Calculator cosines of true bearings handle the signs for you.
ch5_ex8_q14: Position from the tent: east $= 4.12 + 3.31\sin 20^\circ$, north $= 3.31\cos 20^\circ$. The tent lies back towards the south-west, so the answer bearing is between $180^\circ$ and $270^\circ$.
Find the bearing of the walker from the tent (about $059^\circ$), then add $180^\circ$ for the way home.
ch5_ex8_q15: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{8}\right) \approx 21^\circ$ is measured below east, so the bearing is $90^\circ + 21^\circ$. Alternatively, $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right) \approx 69^\circ$ from south gives $180^\circ - 69^\circ$, the same $111^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q16a: Think of it as turning around to face the way you came: that is always a half-turn, $180^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q16b: Adding 180 would go past 360, so subtract instead. A back bearing must always stay between $000^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q17a: Convert to true bearings first: E$12^\circ$S $= 102^\circ$T and S$27^\circ$E $= 153^\circ$T. Then east $= 10\sin 102^\circ + 20\sin 153^\circ$ and north $= 10\cos 102^\circ + 20\cos 153^\circ$.
ch5_ex8_q17b: The boat ends up at about $137^\circ$T from A (south-east), so the way back is $137^\circ + 180^\circ \approx 317^\circ$T, which is north-west.
ch5_ex8_q18a: Choose a scale that makes both lengths whole centimetres. 1 cm = 2 km turns 12 km and 6 km into 6 cm and 3 cm.
ch5_ex8_q18d: The lunch stop is far east and only a little north, so the bearing should be close to $090^\circ$. $083.15^\circ$ fits.
ch5_ex8_q18e: Range check: a straight line home is shorter than the $12 + 6 = 18$ km route taken. It is only slightly longer than the 14.63 km east distance, because the north part is small.
ch5_ex8_q19: Using east $= d\sin(\text{bearing})$ and north $= d\cos(\text{bearing})$ for all three legs avoids drawing three separate quadrant triangles.
The group ends at about $288^\circ$T from base, so home is $288^\circ - 180^\circ = 108^\circ$T.
